title: Past simple: irregular verbs and questions
objectives: Use common irregular past forms in positive statements.
Form questions and negatives with did and a base verb.
Ask for information about finished past events.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: Many common verbs have an irregular past form. This means the past form does not follow the usual regular -ed spelling pattern. For example, go becomes went, see becomes saw and have becomes had. ‘We went to the park yesterday’ describes a finished action. The form went is the same with I, she, we and they.

Irregular verbs are common in everyday conversation. It is useful to learn each base verb and its past form together: go–went, see–saw, have–had, eat–ate, buy–bought, make–made, take–took and come–came. Some verbs have the same written form in the present and past, such as put–put. Context tells us the time.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: In a positive statement, use the past form after the subject: ‘She bought a coat’ or ‘They ate lunch’. Do not add -ed to an irregular form: buy becomes bought, not buyed. Some past forms look similar to the base verb and others look very different. A dictionary or a reliable verb list can help with unfamiliar forms.

For a negative, use did not or didn’t plus the base verb: ‘She didn’t buy a coat’. For a yes/no question, use did + subject + base verb: ‘Did she buy a coat?’ The past meaning is already carried by did. Use the same pattern with all subjects. In short answers, use did or didn’t: ‘Yes, she did’ or ‘No, she didn’t’.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: For more information, put a question word before did: ‘Where did you go?’ and ‘What did they eat?’ A question word can ask about a place, thing, time or person. In this pattern, the subject comes after did and before the main verb. A short answer gives the information: ‘We went to the beach’ or ‘They ate pasta’.

Look at the examples below. Compare ‘He saw the film’ with ‘Did he see the film?’ Saw appears in the positive statement; see follows did in the question. The same change happens in negatives: ‘He didn’t see the film’. The earlier unit explains that be has its own past question pattern: ‘Was he there?’

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Do not use the past form after did in these questions and negatives: say ‘Did you go?’, not ‘Did you went?’ Do not use do or does to ask about a completed past event in this pattern. Use did for every subject, including he and she.

Some questions ask who performed the action: ‘Who saw the film?’ Here who is the subject, and the pattern is different from ‘Who did you see?’ This unit practises questions with an expressed subject after did. The verb read is written the same in present and past, but its pronunciation changes; listen for the difference in context.

examples.sentence: I went to the market yesterday.
examples.note: Went is the past form of go.

examples.sentence: She saw a film last night.
examples.note: Saw is the past form of see.
Had is the past form of have.

examples.sentence: They bought a new table last week.
examples.note: Bought is the past form of buy.

examples.sentence: He didn’t eat lunch at home.
examples.note: Use the base form eat after didn’t.

examples.sentence: Did you take the bus? Yes, I did.
examples.note: Did introduces the question and the short answer.
The question word comes before did and the subject.

examples.sentence: What did they make for dinner?
examples.note: Use the base form make after did and the subject.

common_errors.reason: Buy has the irregular past form bought.
Use the base form go after did.
Use the base form eat after didn’t.

summary: Many common verbs have irregular positive past forms, such as went, saw and bought.
Use did or didn’t with the base verb in ordinary past questions and negatives.
Put a question word before did to ask for information.
